items.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014
items.q: the guy who worked for 15 years or so, Dr. Billy Taylor, Joe Newman, guys like Nathan Davis, some of those pioneers fought for and helped put jazz education in place

ctx.x: It’s ironic because jazz, like in academia now, is flourishing. Every college and, you know, at least has some jazz presence. And also you can major in jazz and so forth. It doesn’t translate to the club scene.

No because some great steps and pioneers put work in on jazz education. You know, the guy who worked for 15 years or so, Dr. Billy Taylor, Joe Newman, guys like Nathan Davis, some of those pioneers fought for and helped put jazz education in place where now most of your major colleges have jazz programs, which at one time, even when I came out of high school that was rare. A lot of schools didn’t have jazz programs. But

now all these schools have jazz programs. So we’ve done a lot to bring along musicians, but we haven’t done enough to bring along people for them to play for. So that’s where we lack. We have to come up now with some thought and some ways of building and replenishing the jazz audience. Getting some people to say look, this is something worthwhile. This is something that we need to have our young people check out. We need to have them grow with.
